title: Graphwise Completeness of the Latent S-ID Algorithm under Selection on Native-Forest Graphs
banked_reason: D0.5 math, decision, citation, and framing checks pass, but the honest NativeForestTrace theorem is subfield below the fixed field floor; unrestricted virtual-edge inverse lifting remains open after all distinct bounded routes were exhausted.
gap_reasons: The proved iff applies only to the note-defined NativeForestTrace subclass, whose load-bearing clause assumes that every terminal obstruction already has nested forests made from actual nonancestor edges.
It therefore bypasses the virtual-edge realization problem central to the published open completeness question and excludes every initial selected-d-separation failure.

Complete the compositional inverse lift for terminal projected forests with shared or branching selection ancestors, preserving one strictly positive selected law and a noncancelling outcome-event contrast.
proof_attempt_summary: The run attacked unrestricted latent S-ID completeness through positive binary inverse lifts, a two-virtual-edge fiber calculation, independent smoothing, affine coding, and a general district extension; these routes either lost positivity/target separation or assumed the common-selected-law crux. It then proved the strongest surviving NativeForestTrace converse using positive finite multistate ordinary-hedge models, common selected-law extension, noncancelling actual-edge routing, and exactification, with all citation and mathematical checks passing. Extending the theorem to projected virtual edges with shared or branching selection ancestors, and handling initial selected-d-separation failures, remains open and is required for field-tier completeness.
tldr: For graphs satisfying \(\operatorname{NativeForestTrace}(G^S;X,Y)\), published latent S-ID Algorithm 1 succeeds if and only if the selected causal query is graphwise identifiable over the full positive exact-graph augmented-SCM class, with models compared only within one finite signature. Success returns Abouei et al.'s Eq. 23 functional. A terminal recursive failure contains an ordinary hedge whose edges are actual edges of \(G^S[N_S]\); Shpitser--Pearl's hedge criterion and KivvaEtAl2022's positive finite-state construction give a full-support multistate separator, and a common randomized-response routing plus finite exactification yields two exact-graph models with the same strictly positive selected law and unequal intervention-before-conditioning targets. Separate finite rank bounds certify graph recursion, and the rational checker is sound for any supplied certificate. The result does not construct binary or rational failure witnesses. Universal virtual-edge completeness, the positive-binary two-virtual-edge separator, initial selected-d-separation failure construction, exact-rational inverse lifting, and total success-or-certificate compilation remain open. The UK Biobank component remains only a conditional two-selector feasibility audit.
gap: AboueiEtAl2024LatentSID proves Algorithm 1 sound and explicitly leaves completeness open. Ordinary hedge completeness does not preserve a normalized selected law when several virtual bidirected edges share or branch through ancestors of \(S\), and no published inverse-lift theorem supplies that missing equality-preserving construction.
fill: The project first proves nonconstancy of the exact binary-signature selected-law fiber on the two-virtual-edge graph, then constructs from every terminal call an explicit record \((F_0,F_1,R,\overline M_0,\overline M_1,x_{\mathrm{bin}})\) with a named local \(D_i=C\) intervention-kernel contrast. It derives an effective rational joint inverse lift, proves that the local contrast survives Eq. 23 placement and selected district extension, and exactifies every parent interface and shared-latent incidence without changing any law. Each failure output is a finite rational table encoding whose realized graph equals the input augmented ADMG, with exact checker evidence and a proved realization in Abouei et al.'s published class. The total graph call count is bounded by the sum of the initial enclosing-component sizes, and the checker has an explicit exhaustive-enumeration operation bound.
